body.text: India likes to think of itself as a vegetarian nation. The data says otherwise—only one in five Indians identifies as vegetarian. In this episode of Frontline Conversations, public health doctor Sylvia Karpagam, author of The Meat of the Matter, argues that this mismatch is not accidental. Drawing on two decades of work at the intersection of nutrition, caste, and policy, she traces how meat and eggs have been stigmatised, taxed with shame, and edited out of health advice—not because science backs the exclusion, but because caste privilege and corporate interest do. From the politics of beef to the myths around protein and cholesterol, Karpagam makes the case that India’s nutritional crisis cannot be solved while its most nutrient-dense, affordable foods remain criminalised.

Let’s start with the title. You call it Meat instead of “non-veg”, which seems like a deliberate choice to stop using vegetarian as the default against which everything else gets defined. How did the idea for this book come about?

Now, actually seeing the response to the book, I’m beginning to think it’s very timely. I think it is a book waiting to happen. Because what we see—at least from the position that I’m in, as a medical doctor and a community medicine professional—is that there’s so much of a mismatch between what research says, the kind of conflict of interest that is playing into research, and then what’s happening at the level of the community.

The vegetarian idea is so mainstream; it’s almost a huge propaganda that is happening in the country, even in the way India is projected outside. Even the EAT-Lancet Commission, which has been pushing for plant-based foods in India without any basic research—they just say, yes, India is primarily a vegetarian country.

I think that myth is very dangerous in many ways. Partly because we don’t distinguish between the kind of vegetarianism of those who are privileged, and finally the kind of policies and programs that trickle down to the poor. It’s a very cheap vegetarianism. And both are clubbed as India’s vegetarians. That’s not what data shows. Data shows that only 20 per cent of Indians actually self-identify as vegetarian.

The fact that you’re calling milk and dairy vegetarian means that you’re benefiting out of animal-sourced foods. And you are labelling certain foods as pure and veg, which fits a caste narrative. You benefit out of it. You allow those foods onto your table, and you see yourself as very superior, very ethical, very pure—but you are also consuming animal-sourced foods. And then you deliberately and very systematically erase and eliminate access to all the other foods. So it’s the politics, it’s the economics, and it’s the caste which plays in. And I think it’s a very big contributor to malnutrition. We don’t actually make those links. The book draws those links.

It talks about the science of nutrition, which has morphed and is misinterpreted. Science shows that liver is the best way to prevent anaemia. But when you actually see how it translates, they’ll say India is primarily vegetarian, and so they’ll be talking about spinach and millets. Even the health education messages have erased a lot of these foods. And it’s not only erasure, it’s also criminalisation—creating shame. People who actually have the knowledge about healthy and nutritious foods are constantly being told, reinforced, that it’s not good for you. It’s like a caste and a corporate nexus. You also have the corporates, the multinationals globally, who are pushing for these kinds of narratives. So it’s to challenge all of that.

The book is densely packed with information but still accessible. What were the challenges?

In medical college, and even now, there’s very little focus given to nutrition per se. So doctors who become social media influencers and act like experts have actually not had basic training in nutrition. Coming from there, one also has to examine one’s own prejudices—things we’ve been told which may not necessarily be true, or which are not actually implemented in practice.

We learn in medicine that the treatment of certain diseases involves animal-sourced foods. But when we come out, we are talking a different language. If most people go to doctors for any illness, they are told to give up meat, which doesn’t come from science. It comes from your own prejudiced understanding of food.

The first draft was very garbled—even I couldn’t read it. I did ask this question a lot to people I trust: Who is this book meant for? Very primarily and centrally, it’s meant for people who’ve constantly been made to feel shame about their food. This book allows people to articulate and feel a sense of pride, and also align it with science.

If you see people in the cities—the elite, the urban, English-speaking, who are working at a policy or program level, or even in civil society—there’s always this language of, oh, people are ignorant, they don’t know, that’s why they’re malnourished. If a woman dies, it’s her own fault because she didn’t take her tablet, she is ignorant, she doesn’t care for her child. That’s the narrative about communities.

It’s also important not to either have this benevolent approach or to romanticise, because romanticising is also a problem. People say the tribal community eats only berries and fruits, they’re very sustainable—which may not necessarily be true. I think we need to be very realistic about the reality of it, and not be top-down benevolent people, because we are actually causing damage and harm. The focus of the book is to link science with people’s practices, and to put the spotlight on the actual barriers to good nutrition. And it’s not either of these groups.

Your book dismantles the idea that protein is just a number that can be replaced—like eggs being replaced by soya. Could you explain what biological value means, and why it matters more than the number of grams of protein?

That’s an important issue, because people have kind of dismantled food into calories, proteins, vitamins, minerals—forgetting that the source matters, the quality matters, and how these foods interact. There is an interaction between foods, between the body and foods, and between different physiological states.

It’s very irritating when you see people on social media rating foods for nutrients—10 for this, 9 for this. Banana, they’ll give 10. Does that mean you have to eat bananas every day? It takes away the economic, cultural, social, and nutritional dimensions, and makes food very ingredient-driven. The problem is that it allows space for the corporates to come in, because then they’ll say, okay, we’ll replace this, or we’ll add iron, or add vitamin A.

Soya is a big thing where everyone’s saying soya has a lot of protein. But as a food group, it belongs to legumes and pulses, and what that food group shares is that they’re difficult to digest and less bioavailable. They contain a lot of phytates, oxalates, and tannins, which prevent absorption of nutrients. If you give a child soya versus an egg, the amount of nutrition the child absorbs is significantly more from the egg. Egg protein is a reference protein—the standard by which other proteins are measured. There is no known standard better than egg protein and breast milk. The fact that soya contains protein doesn’t mean it’s going to be available to the body.

Akshaya Patra Foundation has recently said that in West Bengal, they’ll remove eggs and give soya chunks, and they said that people in Japan eat soya. But the way the Japanese eat soya is very fundamentally different. In Japan, it’s part of a very diverse meal—you will not say, I’ll replace an egg or fish or meat with soya. And the best form soya can be consumed in is if it’s soaked, the milk extracted, or fermented. That is the best form. What we’re doing here is removing the milk and the oils, and whatever fibrous part is left, we’re making into soya chunks and giving that to children. You’re just giving fibre to children. With children—because they have small stomachs and eat less food—each meal should be highly nutrient-dense, which is not going to happen with millets or soya chunks.

In 2015, global dietary advice walked back on dietary cholesterol, saying it’s no longer a nutrient of concern. But the fearmongering hasn’t ceased—Indian doctors still advise against eggs and meat at the slightest spike in cholesterol. Why are clinical practices in India lagging?

This particular guideline aligns with already pre-existing caste prejudices, so it’s convenient to continue upholding that myth. The way the conclusion was reached—that saturated fats are bad, dietary cholesterol is a problem—the research itself is very problematic. It has left out important details. At most it can show some association, but it has not established causation.

Subsequent studies—even in the US—where saturated fats and dietary cholesterol were reduced, it’s not like heart disease or metabolic disease came down. In fact, as these naturally occurring fats came down, metabolic diseases have shown a rise. It’s the opposite correlation. Many of these studies are flawed, and that’s been demonstrated. The decision to withdraw dietary cholesterol as a nutrient of concern came because of the failure to establish causation.

As per sound research, fats and oils should comprise at least 30 per cent of your calorie intake, and about 20-25 per cent should come from proteins. Only about 60 per cent should come from carbohydrates. But in India, most of our calories come from carbohydrates, so our other nutrient needs are not being met. Highly refined, ultra-processed carbohydrates and sugars are what contribute to metabolic disease.

Fats are very important, especially for children. The brain needs a lot of fat for development. Vitamins A, D, E, and K, which are fat-soluble, cannot be absorbed by the body without fat in the diet. It’s needed for nerve development and for regrowth of nerve tissue after injury. If you go to a doctor with any health problem, the first advice is to give up meat, give up eggs—which is very outdated, disproved, and challenged. There’s no evidence that dietary cholesterol and saturated fats are associated with ill health. We need a shift in the medical understanding of fats specifically.

You dedicate an entire chapter to beef—one of the most stigmatised meats in India, with mob lynchings over even the suspicion that someone is carrying it. Yet India is one of the biggest exporters of beef. Why should India destigmatise beef consumption?

India should very seriously consider moving away from religion, caste, prejudice, and mythology, and start focussing on science, and recognise the seriousness of the nutritional crisis in the country. We have high levels of stunting, underweight children, women who are stunted with complications during pregnancy, and adults with obesity, diabetes, and heart disease.

There are about six food groups: cereals and millets; pulses and legumes; fruits and vegetables; fats and oils; eggs, milk and dairy; and meat, poultry, and fish. Each meets different nutritional needs, and their absence causes disadvantages. Right now we are stuck at cereals and millets. People’s idea of diversity is, if you have a problem with rice, go to millets—but that’s the same food group. Diversity is not interchanging within a food group; it’s having a variety from all of them. Unless we have these other food groups, we’re not going to address the nutritional crisis with tablets or fortification. These are like putting a plaster on a big gaping wound.

The politics around beef is very interesting. The vegans who make a big noise about sentient beings are completely quiet about the export industry. The nutritious foods of the country are being monetised to benefit a few who are not the communities consuming these foods, and there’s very little objection to that. You pick some poor Muslim man who’s vulnerable and marginalised—he may or may not have beef, that’s irrelevant—and that becomes your target. They film it, publicise it, and act as though a huge crime has been committed. Even the media uses language like “he was smuggling beef”, participating in the criminalization of what is traditionally eaten by a lot of people.

Beef is cheap, nutrient-dense, and that’s documented by science—not some fictional story or mythology. People who can’t afford fine cuts buy 50 grams of organ meat, and there’s an understanding in communities about its importance. Increasingly, it’s being criminalised. You hear people saying, he was eating beef, so what’s wrong with lynching him. We’ve gone to that extreme of bizarreness when it comes to food. We’re not giving people an alternative; we’re not saying, we’ll make mutton or chicken cheaper. You’re removing an important, affordable food group.

And it’s not only the beef eaters who suffer wherever there’s a cattle slaughter ban—it’s the farmers, the people working in leather, with hooves and gelatin and blood. You cut entire industries and take away livelihoods when you just announce a ban because of a festival, making entire streets meat-free. What if someone wants meat for a wedding at that time?

There’s a study I’ve quoted which shows that wherever cattle slaughter bans are introduced, haemoglobin drops among women in beef-eating communities. We have a crisis of anaemia—not only iron deficiency but B12, zinc, and vitamin A deficiency too. And beef, especially organ meat like liver, is the highest on the scale of nutrient-dense foods for these. We have anaemia of around 56 per cent in the country, contributing to stunting and cognitive deficiencies in children, and it’s the biggest cause of maternal deaths.

The way we’re trying to solve this is with tablets, and by fortifying rice, which has never been proved beneficial. In fact, it’s harmful for people with tuberculosis, malnutrition, infection, thalassemia, or sickle cell anaemia. And then we’re removing all the nutritious foods. From criminalising beef, we’ve now reached a point where we’re not even ready to give eggs to children—people are on the streets saying you can’t give eggs. The vegetarian fragility has become so unsustainable for the rest of the country. Now in colleges they want segregation—separate plates. Sudha Murthy is a good role model for this: she carries separate spoons, and people say, what’s wrong with that, vegetarians just want their tiny space to have their food in peace.

But there’s a politics and economics around it. By saying vegetarian food is superior and must be protected, you are reinforcing discrimination, segregation, prejudice. There was a book brought out for the National Education Policy on wellness that says India has always been sattvic—that Bhima and Hanuman used to eat sattvic food, that India is genetically more suited to vegetarian food. They’ve labelled the foods eaten by communities as tamasic and rajasic, and say “eat what your grandma made”. But that grandma is only one kind—the sattvic, curd-rice-eating, own-spoon-carrying kind. What about the grandma making dry fish and organ meat, whose grandchildren love her red ant chutneys? Those grandmas don’t become the model grandma. We have to recognise that these are very important food groups that, because of this fragility, we are denying to entire communities. That book is specifically for those communities to reclaim pride in their own foods, without romanticising them. Interestingly, people now say, I know one Dalit vegan and one Muslim vegan, therefore veganism is good—but that doesn’t make sense.

You speak of offering medical support after a demolition drive in Bengaluru, where people lost access to homes, drinking water, and sanitation overnight. How did that experience change your understanding of social determinants of health?

Medical textbooks don’t focus a lot on social determinants. We actually saw that when people lost access to toilets, livelihoods, water, and a place to cook, health deteriorated. Children started getting more diarrhoea and respiratory infections, leading to more malnutrition—a vicious cycle they cannot come out of on their own. You need the system to recognise that these children are falling out of all social safety networks.

Same with pregnant women—loss of access to healthcare or nutritious food causes complications, sometimes intergenerational ones. If the mother has anaemia, the child is also more likely to have anaemia. We saw during the COVID-19 pandemic that senior citizens who lost access to balanced foods had worse diabetes and hypertension, and therefore worse COVID-19 outcomes.

Having a curative approach to healthcare without looking at these determinants is not going to help people. It’s going to bring in a model of healthcare that’s less and less accessible. The medical-industrial complex, Big Pharma, and now Big Food, which is suddenly saying it has the solutions to all our food problems. It brings in the issue of food sovereignty, sustainability, culture. Unless these social determinants are addressed, we’re going to have a looming healthcare crisis.

During the demolitions, there was a woman who delivered her baby on the footpath. The baby had an infection, so she went to a nearby clinic, and the doctor told her to give the baby a commercial infant formula, shouting at the mother for not doing so. First, that’s promoting ultra-processed foods. And when the poor leave their own foods for this kind, they end up giving it very dilute to preserve the tin longer, which also causes malnutrition and pushes the child into ultra-processed foods very fast. It shows how disconnected the doctor is—unless you’re aware of where people are coming from, this kind of advice adds to the crisis.
Your book covers the global push for plant-based food, including in India, framed as reducing carbon footprint. Why should we see it differently in the Indian context?

In the Indian context, we are a pastoralist community. The food, especially meats, comes mainly from the pastoralist system. Factory farming is a problem, as is the mass production of anything else, which is what happens with the push for plant-based foods. Billionaires and large companies are buying up large tracts of land and getting into monocropping. The EAT-Lancet Commission, which has a lot of conflicts of interest, is pushing what they call a planetary health diet—one homogeneous diet prescribed for everyone. Interestingly, they don’t say “eat fruits and vegetables”, they say “plant-based”, and most of their products are corn, soya, or peas.

It’s very audacious for humans to say we can replicate meat, because muscle is highly evolved—not something you can manufacture in a lab. You need antibiotics to keep lab meat safe for human consumption. It doesn’t work like that. But they make individuals responsible for climate change and animal welfare, rather than looking at who’s causing the most pollution—the factories, the industries, digital pollution, automobile pollution. People who are already eating meat once a week, who are already malnourished, are the ones being handed the moral burden.

If you ask people to go plant-based or vegan, exports of cashews and almonds from India have increased. Where is the sustainability in suddenly monocropping and exporting these so someone can feel moral in another country? In India, and in many pastoralist communities, there’s a coexistence between plants, livestock, and humans. Farmers say they love their animals but know they’re part of a larger system. They sell them, and only then can they get animals for milk or agriculture. That’s a more pragmatic understanding than people who sit in cities, English-speaking, saying, I love animals.

Earlier, there was the criminalisation of saturated fats and cholesterol, and we’ve still not come out of that corporate-pushed agenda. Now they’ve come up with plant-based. If you’re doing monocropping, what happens to the soil, to biodiversity? There are other experts who’ve gone deeper into this, but the book tries to bring out questions for people to think about. When we fortify rice, we don’t have the pre-fortifying mix in India—we ship it from other countries. What does that do to food sovereignty, to air miles? And we’re parallelly exporting our nutritious foods, making them unavailable here. There’s a politics and an economics to it that we need to recognize.
